2 years

3 years

caption: Is your child talking late? Here is what most children do at 12 months, 18 months, 2 years and 3 years. It is a guide, not a diagnosis, and a hearing check always comes first. The full age-by-age guide is on our website.

headline: Meltdown or tantrum?
sub: They look the same. They need different help.
points: Has a goal
Is overload, with no goal
Checks your face
Words do not get through
Stops when the goal is met
Ends in exhaustion
Stay calm, hold the line
Fewer words, less noise
note: The same child can have both.
alt: Infographic: meltdown or tantrum? A tantrum has a goal, the child checks your face, and it stops when the goal is met; stay calm and hold the line. A meltdown is overload with no goal, words do not get through, and it ends in exhaustion; use fewer words and less noise. The same child can have both.
caption: A tantrum has a goal. A meltdown is overload. They look almost the same from the outside, and they need different things from you. Here is how to tell them apart in the moment. The full guide is on our website.
scene: WHAT IS HAPPENING: a boy of about four sits on the ground hugging his knees, looking down with a small frown; his father kneels calmly beside him at his level, patient and gentle, one hand resting open on his own knee, simply staying close. A soft toy rabbit lies on the ground next to the boy.

headline: Too many languages?
sub: Bangla at home, English at school, and late talking
points: Two languages are why he is talking late.
Two languages do not cause speech delay.
Mixing Bangla and English means confusion.
Mixing is normal. He uses the word he knows.
Drop Bangla. Speak only English at home.
English is built on a rich home language.
note: A delay across both languages is still worth checking.
alt: Infographic: too many languages? Myth: too many languages are why your child is talking late. Fact: growing up with 2 languages does not cause speech delay. Myth: mixing Bangla and English in one sentence means confusion. Fact: mixing is normal, your child reaches for the word he knows best. Myth: drop Bangla and speak only English at home. Fact: a rich home language is the foundation English gets built on. A delay across both languages is still worth checking.
caption: Bangla with the grandparents, English at school, and a child who is not talking much yet. Parents are often told to pick one language, but growing up with two does not cause speech delay, and dropping Bangla fixes nothing. The full guide, including how to count words across both languages, is on our website.

note: Most 4-year-olds have gaps. Pick 2 items, not 10.
alt: Infographic: is my child ready for school? It is mostly habits, not the alphabet. Says goodbye at the gate and goes in. Sits at a table for 5 to 10 minutes. Follows a 2-step instruction. Waits about 1 minute for a turn. Asks for help with words, a gesture or a picture. Most 4-year-olds have gaps; pick 2 items, not 10.
caption: Admission season makes every parent wonder about the alphabet. School readiness is mostly sitting, listening and asking for help, and those are ordinary habits you can practise at home. The full checklist is on our website.

Her mother kneels beside her, holding a small plain school bag ready and waiting patiently without helping, with a proud little smile. The girl's other shoe sits on the ground next to her.

headline: Why are loud rooms so hard?
sub: Three sensory patterns that show up often
points: Over
Flinches, covers up or runs
Under
Does not react to a call
Seeking
Crashes, jumps and chews for input
At home
Heavy work first: 10 big jumps
note: Most children are a mixture, and it shifts with tiredness.
alt: Infographic: why are loud rooms so hard? Three sensory patterns that show up often. Over-responsive: the volume is turned up, so a child flinches, covers up or runs. Under-responsive: the volume is turned down, with no reaction to a call. Seeking: the child goes looking for input by crashing, jumping or chewing. At home: heavy work before the hard part, such as 10 big jumps. Most children are a mixture, and it shifts with tiredness.
caption: Loud weddings, scratchy labels and haircuts are hard work for some children, and it is not stubbornness. Sensory processing is how the brain sorts what comes in from the body and the world, and three patterns show up again and again. The full guide, with 5 things to try at home, is on our website.
scene: WHAT IS HAPPENING: a girl of about six leans forward and pushes a loaded cane laundry basket along the ground with both hands, her face set with happy effort. Her father walks one step behind her, bending slightly with his hands open, cheering her on quietly. A folded cotton towel sits on top of the basket.

headline: My child cannot sit still
sub: Start from the length your child can manage
points: Watch for 3 days to find your child's real limit
Practise only that length, and end there
Hold it for about a week, then add 30 seconds
End while it is going well. Praise the sitting.
note: Expect bad days. Drop the length, keep the routine.
alt: Infographic: my child cannot sit still. Start from the length your child can manage. One: watch for 3 days to find your child's real limit. Two: practise only that length, and end there. Three: hold it for about a week, then add 30 seconds. Four: end while it is going well, and praise the sitting. Expect bad days; drop the length and keep the routine.
caption: Pushing for five more minutes almost never works, because sitting and attending are physical skills built from a length your child can already manage. Start shorter than you think is useful, and stop while things are still going well. The full guide is on our website.
scene: WHAT IS HAPPENING: a boy of about six sits on a cushion at a small low wooden table, fitting a piece into a simple wooden puzzle. His father sits beside him, pointing gently at a small sand timer on the table whose sand has nearly run through. Both look calm and pleased.
